title: The Lord God: Sovereign Over The Nations
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Context of American Independence
subpoints: The spirit of independence as a national strength and weakness
The tension between unalienable rights and historical failures
The danger of relegating God to a national mascot

outline.title: The Universal Lordship of Christ
subpoints: Christ bears the name Yahweh, above every name
Every knee in heaven, earth, and under the earth will bow
Submission to Christ is inevitable, either by grace or judgment

outline.title: God's Sovereignty in Old Testament History
subpoints: Nations as tools in God's hands (Medes, Assyria, Babylon)
The fall of superpowers who rebelled against God
The destruction of the Assyrian army before Jerusalem

outline.title: The Basis of National Judgment
subpoints: Righteousness exalts a nation; sin brings reproach
God changes times and seasons, removing and raising kings
The consistency of God's character in judgment and blessing

outline.title: The Ultimate Fulfillment in Christ
subpoints: The government is upon the shoulders of the Messiah
The kingdoms of this world become the kingdom of the Lord
Christ's eternal reign over all nations

summary:
This sermon explores the theological and historical implications of God's sovereignty over the nations, particularly in the context of the United States approaching its 250th anniversary. The speaker contrasts the American spirit of independence with the biblical truth that all nations are ultimately answerable to God. While acknowledging the positive aspects of national freedom and opportunity, the message warns against reducing God to a cultural symbol or mascot, emphasizing that He is the sovereign ruler who will call every nation to account.

The exposition centers on Philippians 2:5-11, highlighting the exaltation of Jesus Christ to the name above every name, identified as Yahweh. It is asserted that every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth will bow to Christ, a reality that will be met either through voluntary submission to the gospel or through the weight of divine judgment. This universal lordship is illustrated through Old Testament examples where God used superpowers like Assyria and Babylon as instruments of His will, ultimately bringing them down for their rebellion.

The sermon concludes by affirming that the basis for national judgment is righteousness versus sin, citing Proverbs and Jeremiah. It points to the fulfillment of this sovereignty in Christ, who bears the government of all nations upon His shoulders. The final hope is presented in Revelation, where the kingdoms of this world become the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ, who reigns forever.
